newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists vow to keep all of France Telecom.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists vow to keep all of France Telecom.

text.p: The opposition Socialists, taking a tough stand on privatisation ahead of the French parliamentary election, vowed on Tuesday to ditch the planned partial sale of France Telecom they won power.

The party which polls suggest is gaining on the ruling centre-right in the run-up to the May/June two-stage vote, would abandon the sale of 30 to 35 percent of the telecommunications giant because it would mean "abandoning the principle of public service," Socialist spokesman Francois Hollande said.
Spelling out the party's privatisation stand, he said it was committed to maintaining "100 percent public ownership" of France Telecom, the Post Office, power utility EDF-GDF and railway SNCF.

Finance Minister Jean Arthuis reacted swiftly to the statements, saying the government was counting on the money from the France Telecom sale to recapitalise ailing state firms. Analysts say the state could reap between 48 and 73.5 billion francs ($12.6 billion) from the planned sale of 30 to 35 percent.
"The state has a duty to recapitalise these firms and we know big amounts are needed this year," Arthuis said. Among those due to get handouts are insurer GAN and arms maker GIAT.
The government has delayed the France Telecom sale, France's biggest-ever stock market operation, until the election is over, but has promised to relaunch it on June 6.

One telecommunications analyst said not privatising France Telecom would have little operational effect on France Telecom as the government "was still going to be the main shareholder and nothing will change the fact it will face full competition when the European telecoms market is liberalised on January 1."
Under Maastricht treaty rules spelling out entry conditions for the European single currency, France cannot use privatisation proceeds to limit its budget deficit this year.
The biggest implication of the Socialist platform was for the long-term health of the French economy, economists said.

The Socialist stand was a far cry from the pro-market attitude of Britain's Labour prime minister, Tony Blair. "This is not Tony Blair-style Socialism committed to keeping the best of Thatcherism. This is not even soft capitalism. This is unreformed Socialism," said Paul Horne of Smith Barney.
"If you want the economy to move you need to oil the wheels and privatisation is clearly a big step toward that," said Sonja Gibbs of Nomura.
The French party's privatisation stand followed its announcement on Monday it would scrap a law passed last February introducing private pension funds.
To lower record 12.8 percent unemployment, it has vowed to cut the work week to 35 hours from 39 with no loss of pay and create 700,000 jobs, half of them in the public sector.
The party's privatisation stand harks back to 1988 when late Socialist President Francois Mitterrand introduced the "ni-ni" doctrine -- no more privatisations, no more nationalisations.
"Our philosphy is indeed the 'ni-ni' policy," said Pierre Moscovici, who helped formulate the party's latest manifesto.

The Socialists backtracked on their anti-privatisation policy in 1991 under former prime minister Michel Rocard after the vast state-controlled sector was so starved of capital it needed access to private sector funds.
He allowed firms to buy minority stakes in state-owned companies under what was called the "breathing space law".
In 1993, when the centre-right took power in parliament, it launched a new drive to sell off state-owned companies.

After conservative President Jacques Chirac announced the snap vote to give him a free hand in the runup to the single currency, Socialist leader Lionel Jospin said he opposed privatising France Telecom, Thomson-CSF and Air France.

But analysts had thought the Socialists were softening their hard line after recent statements by party bosses. Former Socialist labour minister Martine Aubry said on Sunday the party did not want the state "to lose its majority in France Telecom".
Hollande said the Socialists did not rule out privatising firms which had no public service role, saying realism should be the guide. "We need to keep a certain flexibility" he said.
But he reiterated the party's opposition to privatisation of state-owned electronics firm Thomson-CSF, adding the party would "maintain public control" of the defence industry.
He did not say whether the Socialists would proceed with the government's plans to privatise troubled state-owned bank Credit Lyonnais. ($ = 5.831 French Francs)
